name: Read values and totals
statement: \text{Read the needed cells/bars, add row or column totals, compare or rank}
derivation: Underline the exact rows, columns and years the question names; ignore the rest of the table.
When a quantity is a difference of two columns (absent $=$ total $-$ present), add each column first and subtract once: $\sum(T_i-P_i)=\sum T_i-\sum P_i$.
Write the derived row or column total beside the table, one number per year or item.
Answer the comparison asked (highest, second highest, ratio) from that one list.
visual_proof: The table with an extra derived column (absentees = Total − Present, summed over the centres) written beside each year; the ranking is read straight down that column.
shortcut: Difference of totals = total of differences: add the Total column and the Present column for a year, then subtract once.
common_traps: Ranking by the Total or Present column instead of absentees: second highest becomes 2020 (C).
Answering the highest (2018, option A) when the second highest is asked.
Reading one centre's columns only instead of summing P, Q and R.

diagram.alt_text: Table of total and present candidates summed over centres P, Q and R for 2016 to 2020, with an absentees column: 19, 30, 34, 31, 30; 2019 is second highest.

verification.code:
import random
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    rows, cols = random.randint(2, 6), random.randint(2, 4)
    tot = [[random.randint(10, 200) for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]
    pres = [[random.randint(0, t) for t in r] for r in tot]
    by_cell = [sum(t - p for t, p in zip(rt, rp)) for rt, rp in zip(tot, pres)]
    by_cols = [sum(rt) - sum(rp) for rt, rp in zip(tot, pres)]
    assert by_cell == by_cols                      # sum of differences = difference of sums
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-09_0900_Q16: (Total, Present) for P, Q, R
data = {2016: [(45, 42), (56, 45), (55, 50)], 2017: [(50, 45), (75, 55), (45, 40)],
        2018: [(64, 60), (65, 45), (65, 55)], 2019: [(80, 69), (84, 72), (70, 62)],
        2020: [(55, 44), (80, 66), (90, 85)]}
absent = {y: sum(t for t, _ in v) - sum(p for _, p in v) for y, v in data.items()}
assert absent == {2016: 19, 2017: 30, 2018: 34, 2019: 31, 2020: 30}
rank = sorted(absent, key=absent.get, reverse=True)
assert rank[1] == 2019 and absent[2019] not in (absent[2018], absent[2020], absent[2017])
opts = {"A": 2018, "B": 2019, "C": 2020, "D": 2017}
assert [k for k, y in opts.items() if y == rank[1]] == ["B"]
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Averages from a chart
statement: \text{average}=\frac{\text{sum of selected values}}{\text{count}};\ \text{compare averages via totals when counts are equal}
derivation: Average $=\frac{\text{sum}}{\text{count}}$ (see [[f:average.arithmetic-mean]]).
If every group has the same count $n$, dividing all totals by $n$ keeps their order, so rank the totals directly.
To add faster, pick a base $b$ near the values: average $=b+\frac{\sum(x_i-b)}{n}$.
With unequal counts, compute each average separately before comparing or combining.
visual_proof: A table of four companies over four years with a deviation-from-240 row under each column: +5, +7, −15, 0; the largest deviation total marks the largest average.
shortcut: Equal counts: compare totals (or sums of deviations from a round base) instead of averages.

steps: Each company has 4 years, so compare totals.

common_traps: Picking the company with the single biggest year (C1's 248 or C4's 248) instead of the biggest total: gives C1 or C4.
Comparing averages over different counts by totals: wrong when one group has more items.
Averaging two averages directly when the groups have different counts; use the combined total over the combined count.

diagram.alt_text: Table of T-shirt production (thousands) for C1 to C4 in 2019 to 2022 with totals 965, 967, 945, 960 and deviation sums from 240 of +5, +7, −15, 0.

name: Percentages and percent change from a chart
conditions: $V_1 \neq 0$ for a percent change ($V_1$ is the base)
derivation: A share is a part over its whole: $\frac{\text{value}}{\text{total}}\times100$ (see [[f:percentage.percent-of-quantity]]).
Change is measured against the starting value: $\%\Delta=\frac{V_2-V_1}{V_1}\times100$ (see [[f:percentage.percent-change]]).
Equivalently $\%\Delta=\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}-1\right)\times100$, quick when $V_2/V_1$ is a clean fraction.
For 'who scored $x\%$', turn $x\%$ into a target total first ($x\%$ of maximum), then match totals.
visual_proof: One student's row of five marks out of 100 added to 395 beside the target 79% of 500 = 395.
shortcut: Convert the percent to a target value once ($79\%$ of $500=395$), then scan the totals instead of dividing each one.
common_traps: Using the new value as the base for % change: gives a smaller % rise than the true one.
Averaging the five subject percentages without checking every subject is out of the same maximum.
Dividing by the wrong total (one subject's maximum 100 instead of 500).

diagram.alt_text: Bar model of 500 maximum marks split into Tarun's 395 (79%) and the 105 marks he missed (21%).

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    vals = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 6))]
    total = sum(vals)
    shares = [F(v, total) * 100 for v in vals]
    assert sum(shares) == 100
    v1, v2 = random.randint(1, 1000), random.randint(0, 2000)
    pct = F(v2 - v1, v1) * 100
    assert pct == (F(v2, v1) - 1) * 100            # shortcut: ratio minus 1
    assert v1 * (1 + pct / 100) == v2              # recovers V2
    p = random.randint(1, 100)
    assert (F(p, 100) * total == sum(vals)) == (p == 100)
    n += 1
# boundary: V1 = 0 has no percent change; total = 0 has no share
for bad in [(0, 5), (0, 0)]:
    try:
        F(bad[1] - bad[0], bad[0]) * 100
        raise AssertionError
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        pass
try:
    F(3, 0)
    raise AssertionError
except ZeroDivisionError:
    pass
assert F(5 - 1, 1) * 100 == 400                    # tiny V1 gives huge %: base matters
# worked example 2024-09-09_0900_Q08: 79% of 5 x 100 marks
marks = {"Tarun": [65, 80, 75, 85, 90], "Rohit": [69, 76, 80, 88, 94], "Mohit": [73, 84, 77, 90, 95],
         "Shobhit": [76, 85, 76, 86, 78], "Sumit": [90, 88, 78, 82, 68]}
target = F(79, 100) * 500
assert target == 395
hit = [s for s, m in marks.items() if sum(m) == target]
assert hit == ["Tarun"]
assert {s: F(sum(m), 500) * 100 for s, m in marks.items()}["Tarun"] == 79
opts = {"A": "Rohit", "B": "Tarun", "C": "Mohit", "D": "Sumit"}
assert [k for k, s in opts.items() if s in hit] == ["B"]
print(f"CASES={n}")
print("BOUNDARY_OK")

name: Ratios from a chart
derivation: Read each named bar; write the two groups as separate sums.
Ratio $=\Sigma A:\Sigma B$; never add or cancel across the colon before summing each side.
Bars on a common scale (all multiples of 25, 50, ...) can be divided by that scale first: $\sum ka_i:\sum kb_i=\sum a_i:\sum b_i$.
Cancel the HCF to lowest terms (see [[f:ratio-proportion.simplify-ratio]]).
visual_proof: A grouped bar chart of Institutes A and B, 2018 to 2022; the three B bars named and the three A bars named are summed into 925 and 700.
shortcut: Divide every bar by the common step first (here 25): $(14+15+8):(6+12+10)=37:28$.
common_traps: Writing the ratio the wrong way round (A : B): gives 28 : 37, option B.
Reading B's 2018 bar (210) or A's 2022 bar (225) for the wrong year.
Simplifying each pair year by year and adding the ratios instead of adding the values.

diagram.alt_text: Grouped bar chart of students enrolled in Institutes A and B from 2018 to 2022: A 150, 275, 300, 250, 225; B 210, 350, 375, 300, 200.

verification.code:
import random
from math import gcd
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    k = random.choice([5, 10, 25, 50])
    a = [k * random.randint(1, 80) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 4))]
    b = [k * random.randint(1, 80) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 4))]
    sa, sb = sum(a), sum(b)
    g = gcd(sa, sb)
    # shortcut: divide every bar by the common scale k first, then add
    sa_k, sb_k = sum(x // k for x in a), sum(x // k for x in b)
    g2 = gcd(sa_k, sb_k)
    assert (sa // g, sb // g) == (sa_k // g2, sb_k // g2)
    assert F(sa, sb) == F(sa // g, sb // g)
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-09_1230_Q20
A = {2018: 150, 2019: 275, 2020: 300, 2021: 250, 2022: 225}
B = {2018: 210, 2019: 350, 2020: 375, 2021: 300, 2022: 200}
num = B[2019] + B[2020] + B[2022]
den = A[2018] + A[2020] + A[2021]
assert (num, den) == (925, 700)
g = gcd(num, den)
r = (num // g, den // g)
assert r == (37, 28)
opts = {"A": (11, 28), "B": (28, 37), "C": (37, 28), "D": (28, 11)}
assert [k for k, v in opts.items() if v == r] == ["C"]
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Derived quantities from given relations
statement: \text{Combine table values with a stated relation (e.g. income}=\text{expenditure}\times(1+p)) \text{ to find the unknown}
derivation: Copy the relation the question gives, e.g. income $=E+E\times\frac{p}{100}$.
Factor out the table value: income $=E\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)$, one multiplication.
Run it backwards when the unknown is the table value: $E=\frac{\text{income}}{1+p/100}$.
When two unknowns are linked (one is twice the other), write one variable, form one equation and solve.
visual_proof: A bar model: expenditure 50 plus a profit piece of 55% of 50 = 27.5, together making income 77.5.
shortcut: Income $=E\times(1+p/100)$: one multiplier, e.g. $55\%$ profit means $\times1.55$.
common_traps: Reading Company B's or A's column for 2003 (15 or 30) instead of C's.
Taking profit alone ($27.5$) as the income.
Treating profit% as a share of income: $50/0.45\approx111.1$, which matches no option.

diagram.alt_text: Bar model: Company C 2003 expenditure 50 crore plus profit 27.5 crore (55% of 50) equals income 77.5 crore.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    e = F(random.randint(1, 10000), random.choice([1, 2, 4, 10]))
    p = F(random.randint(-99, 300))
    income = e + e * p / 100
    assert income == e * (1 + p / 100)             # one multiplier
    assert income / (1 + p / 100) == e             # reverse: expenditure from income
    assert (income - e) / e * 100 == p             # profit% recovered
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-19_1600_Q09: Company C, 2003
exp_c, prof_c = 50, F(55)
inc = exp_c * (1 + prof_c / 100)
assert inc == F(155, 2)
opts = {"A": F(775, 10), "B": F(757, 10), "C": F(698, 10), "D": F(105)}
assert [k for k, v in opts.items() if v == inc] == ["A"]
# second case 2024-09-19_1600_Q16: 0.7x + 0.8(2x) = 552
x = F(552) / (F(7, 10) + F(8, 10) * 2)
assert x == 240 and 2 * x == 480
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Pie chart central angles
derivation: The whole pie is $100\%$ and $360^\circ$, so $1\%=3.6^\circ$.
A sector of $p\%$ has angle $\theta=3.6p^\circ$.
A sector of $\theta^\circ$ holds $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of the total.
Comparisons between sectors (ratio, % more or less) need only the angles or percents; the total cancels.
visual_proof: A pie split into 20%, 40%, 30% and 10% sectors; the 20% and 30% sectors together cover half the circle, 180°.
shortcut: $1\%=3.6^\circ$; $25\%=90^\circ$, $50\%=180^\circ$. Ignore the total when only angles or comparisons are asked.
common_traps: Converting 1200 fruits into counts first and dividing wrongly: wastes time and invites slips.
Taking apples alone ($72^\circ$) or oranges alone ($108^\circ$).
Using $1\%=3.6$ backwards ($50/3.6$) when the chart is already in percent.

diagram.alt_text: Strip of 360 degrees split into Apples 72°, Bananas 144°, Oranges 108° and Sweet lime 36°; Apples plus Oranges make 180°.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    parts = [random.randint(1, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 7))]
    s = sum(parts)
    pct = [F(p, s) * 100 for p in parts]
    ang = [q / 100 * 360 for q in pct]
    assert sum(ang) == 360
    for q, a in zip(pct, ang):
        assert a == q * F(18, 5)                   # 1% = 3.6 degrees
    total = random.randint(1, 10**6)
    vals = [a / 360 * total for a in ang]
    assert sum(vals) == total
    i, j = random.sample(range(len(parts)), 2)
    # comparisons need no total: ratio of values = ratio of angles
    assert vals[i] / vals[j] == ang[i] / ang[j]
    assert (vals[i] - vals[j]) / vals[j] == (ang[i] - ang[j]) / ang[j]
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-13_0900_Q20: apples 20%, oranges 30%; total 1200 not needed
theta = F(20 + 30, 100) * 360
assert theta == 180
opts = {"A": 90, "B": 180, "C": 220, "D": 160}
assert [k for k, v in opts.items() if v == theta] == ["B"]
# second case 2024-09-18_1230_Q11 (degrees only)
btr, csh = 45 + 65 + 25, 100 + 60 + 30
assert round(float(F(csh - btr, csh) * 100), 2) == 28.95
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Pie chart percent to value
derivation: A sector of $p\%$ holds $\frac{p}{100}\times$ total.
The gap between two sectors is $\frac{p_1}{100}T-\frac{p_2}{100}T=\frac{p_1-p_2}{100}T$: subtract percents first.
A part of a sector ($q\%$ of a $p\%$ sector) is $\frac{pq}{10^4}T$.
The rest of a sector is $(100-q)\%$ of it.
visual_proof: A bar for 20,000 employees with department D's 30% piece (6000) split into 30% female (1800) and 70% male (4200).
common_traps: Answering the department size (6000) instead of the males.
Finding females (1800) and stopping.
Taking 70% of the whole company: 14000.

diagram.alt_text: Bar model: 20,000 employees with department D as 30% = 6000; D split into 1800 females (30%) and 4200 males (70%).

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    total = random.randint(1, 10**6)
    p1, p2 = random.randint(0, 100), random.randint(0, 100)
    v1, v2 = F(p1, 100) * total, F(p2, 100) * total
    assert v1 - v2 == F(p1 - p2, 100) * total      # difference straight from percents
    q = random.randint(0, 100)
    # q% of a sector: multiply the two percents
    assert F(q, 100) * v1 == F(p1 * q, 10**4) * total
    assert F(100 - q, 100) * v1 == v1 - F(q, 100) * v1
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-12_1230_Q06: D = 30% of 20000; 30% of D female
total, d = 20000, 30
dept = F(d, 100) * total
assert dept == 6000
male = F(70, 100) * dept
assert male == 4200 == F(d * 70, 10**4) * total
opts = {"A": 4500, "B": 4000, "C": 5000, "D": 4200}
assert [k for k, v in opts.items() if v == male] == ["D"]
print(f"CASES={n}")
